title: Ignatius on the road
hook: chained on his way to the lions, he writes that he is God's wheat (Romans 4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clement's letter to quarreling Corinth, and your line was let the proud be humbled.

A prisoner is being marched overland toward Rome, chained to a squad of soldiers. He calls them ten leopards, and says they only get worse when they're treated kindly. He is Ignatius; in his letters he calls himself the bishop of Syria, and tradition places his church in Antioch. He is going to Rome to die in the arena. Along the road, Christians come out to meet him in the towns he passes, and he writes letters to their churches. One goes ahead of him, to the Christians in Rome, and it's a strange letter. It's a request: please, don't save me.

Ignatius worries that the Roman Christians will try to step in. So he writes, in effect: say nothing on my behalf. Then comes the picture that gives today its line. I am God's wheat, he writes, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may be found pure bread of Christ. Wheat isn't finished when it's harvested. It has to be ground before it can feed anyone. Some readers hear an echo of Jesus in John's Gospel: "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." And for Christians who share bread at the Lord's table, the picture of becoming bread is hard to miss. Readers hear this letter in different ways. Some are moved by a man so sure of Christ that he walks toward the arena without flinching. Some are uneasy, and ask whether he wanted death too much. Both take the letter seriously. And notice the rest of the road. A condemned man, with every reason to think only of himself, spends his last journey writing to other people's churches: be united, gather together often, care for the widows, be patient with one another. Letter by letter, he was already becoming bread for people he would never see again.

Bread is ordinary: it gets broken, shared, eaten, gone. Bring to mind the people your days feed in some way, the ones you cook for, work for, listen to, look after, and picture each one for a breath, along with what in you is being ground down right now, tiredness, patience, time, that could still feed someone. If you pray, offer your day to God as bread; if you don't, simply hold the people who depend on you.
Ignatius. A bishop chained on the way to Rome, writing to churches as he goes, and asking the Romans to let him become God's wheat.
Your line: god's wheat. Ground first, and then shared with others. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches remember Ignatius of Antioch as a saint and martyr, and his letters are read today among the writings of the Apostolic Fathers.

chat.says: What did Ignatius mean by calling himself God's wheat?
options: Wheat is ground before it feeds anyone; he hoped to become bread of Christ.
He meant he had been a farmer before he became a bishop in Syria.
He meant the church in Rome would grow as big as a field of wheat.

Ignatius is paraphrased throughout (Lightfoot's translation not verified word for word): 'ten leopards' who grow worse when treated kindly (Romans 5); 'bishop of Syria' (Romans 2); his request that the Romans not intervene (Romans 1–2, 4); 'I am God's wheat... pure bread of Christ' (Romans 4). Check each.
'Tradition places his church in Antioch': Eusebius and later tradition; confirm.
The bread/Eucharist echo is offered as 'hard to miss' for Christians who share bread at the Lord's table; churches understand the Eucharist differently, and the script does not take a side.
The summary of his advice ('be united, gather together often, care for the widows, be patient with one another') draws from To the Ephesians 13 and To Polycarp 1, 4; confirm.
